block_text_edits.old: Wages can be shown on a diagram with the wage rate on the vertical axis and the quantity of labour on the horizontal axis. The demand curve for labour slopes downwards and the supply curve slopes upwards; the equilibrium wage is where they cross. Higher demand for the product shifts labour demand to the right and raises the wage. More trained workers shift labour supply to the right and lower the wage. Strong trade unions (topic 2.2) may push wages above this level through collective bargaining, and a legal minimum wage (topic 6.3) sets a floor.

block.heading: The labour market on a diagram
block.text:
Draw the wage rate on the vertical axis and the quantity of labour on the horizontal axis. Labour demand slopes downwards, labour supply upwards, and the equilibrium wage is where they cross. In a coastal town, guest houses want 150 housekeepers at N$25 an hour and 150 will work for that wage. More tourists then raise the demand for rooms and so for housekeepers, because labour demand is derived demand: guest houses want 100 more at every wage. Labour demand shifts right, from D1 to D2; supply does not move. The wage rises to N$30 and employment to 200.

![Housekeeper labour market](diagrams/item-6145-4.2-025-proc-answer.png)

More trained workers would instead shift supply right and lower the wage. Strong trade unions (topic 2.2) may push wages above equilibrium, and a legal minimum wage (topic 6.3) sets a floor.

item.prompt: In a coastal town, guest houses want 250, 200, 150, 100 and 50 housekeepers at wages of N$15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 an hour (D1), and 50, 100, 150, 200 and 250 people are willing to work at those wages (S), as in the diagram. More tourists visit the town, and guest houses now want 100 more housekeepers at every wage. Use the diagram to show the original and new equilibrium wage and employment, and explain which curve shifts (4).
item.canonical_answer: The original equilibrium E1 is where D1 crosses S: N$25 an hour and 150 housekeepers. More tourists increase the demand for guest-house rooms, and labour demand is derived from that demand, so labour demand shifts right by 100 at every wage, from D1 to D2 (350, 300, 250, 200 and 150 housekeepers at N$15 to N$35). Labour supply does not shift, because nothing has changed the number of people willing to work at each wage. The new equilibrium E2, where D2 crosses S, is N$30 an hour and 200 housekeepers. The wage rises by N$5 an hour and employment by 50, less than the shift of 100, because the higher wage reduces the number guest houses want and draws more people into the work.
